# The Day My Van Almost Caught Fire (and What I Wish I'd Checked)

This isn't a fun one. No before-and-after doodle pics today, sorry.

I've rewritten the start of this post about six times because I don't really know how to begin, so I'll just say it. Two weeks ago my van almost caught fire in the middle of a groom. Everyone is fine. Moose is fine. I'm fine, mostly. But the van is off the road for at least three more weeks, and I've been going a bit out of my mind.

I'm writing this up properly for two reasons. First, a few of you have messaged asking what happened, and I'd rather explain it once, carefully, than forty times badly over text. Second, and this is the big one, my friend Tasha is about to put a deposit down on a build with the same guy who built mine. Tasha, this one's for you. And for anyone else in the groomer group chat who's dreaming about going mobile or already has a van they've never really looked under the bench of.

**Before anything else: I am not an electrician.** I groom dogs. Everything technical in here is what a real marine electrician explained and showed me, plus what I've read since trying to understand it. I've done my best to get the numbers right, but please don't use this post as a wiring guide. Use it as a list of questions to ask, and then get a professional to look at your van.

## What happened

It was Wednesday, October 28th, around 2:15 in the afternoon. I was parked in a client's driveway in Bedford, drying Moose. If you don't know Moose, he's a Bernese mountain dog, which means he's roughly the size of a loveseat and holds water like one too. I had the dryer cranked on high, because with a Berner you either commit or you're there until dinner.

I smelled hot plastic first. Honestly my first thought was the dryer motor, because those things work hard and they do get a bit smelly sometimes. I was actually looking at the dryer when I noticed smoke coming out of the bench seat. That's where my batteries live.

I'd love to tell you I was calm. What actually happened is my brain went completely white for maybe a second, and then I did the things. I killed the battery switch. I got Moose out the side door. He was still damp and absolutely thrilled about it, doing zoomies on his own front lawn like he'd been released from prison. Then I grabbed the extinguisher and gave the area a bit of a blast. I'm honestly not sure I even needed to, since once the switch was off the smoke started dying down pretty fast. But I wasn't about to stand there and find out.

When it was safe to look, the lug on the end of the positive cable (the metal connector that bolts the cable on) was black. The plastic jacket on the cable had melted back about 3cm from the end.

Moose's mom came out with a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I'm not exaggerating, my hands were going. I'll never forget that. She didn't make it a big thing, she just sat there with me. If you're reading this, thank you. Moose's next groom is on me forever.

## My setup, for context

So you know what I was running:

- 3000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries
- 12V system
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren), spring 2025

I want to say something about this up front. **I'm not trying to trash Darren publicly.** I'm going to lay out what the electrician found, factually, and people can make up their own minds. For what it's worth, I've sent him three texts and an email since it happened and haven't heard back yet. That's just where things are.

## What the electrician found

After the van was towed, I got Priya from Sackville Marine Electric to go through it. She was amazing and also very honest, which is what I needed even when it stung.

There were three main problems. I'll go through them the way she explained them to me.

### 1. The main cable was too small

The cable running from the battery to the inverter was 4 AWG. Priya said for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system, it should have been 2/0.

If you're like me and wire sizes mean nothing to you, here's the part that matters: with wire gauge, **a smaller number means a thicker wire.** 2/0 (you say it "two-aught" or "double-aught") is a lot thicker than 4 AWG. Not a little thicker. Noticeably chunkier. And thicker wire can carry more current without heating up.

Here's the math, which was the part that really clicked for me. Amps = watts ÷ volts.

- My dryer pulls somewhere around 1800–2000W.
- At 12V, 2000W ÷ 12V = about 167 amps.
- Inverters also lose a bit of power converting from battery to wall-style power, so the real draw from the battery is a bit higher than that.
- Sometimes I've got the water heater going at the same time as the dryer, and that's when it really adds up.

So depending on what I was running, that one cable was carrying somewhere in the range of **150 to 250 amps.** And if the inverter ever ran close to its full 3000W, that's 3000 ÷ 12 = 250 amps before you even count the losses.

That's the thing about a 12V system that I didn't really get before. A 2000W dryer plugged into the wall at a salon is no big deal, because the wall is 120V and it's only pulling around 17 amps. Run that same dryer off 12V batteries and the cable between the battery and the inverter is carrying about ten times the current. That's why those cables have to be so thick.

### 2. The crimp on the lug was bad

This is the one that made me feel sick.

The lug on the positive end of that cable hadn't been crimped with a proper crimping tool. Priya said it looked like it had been squished on with pliers or a hammer. A proper crimp squeezes the metal evenly all the way around the wire so it's basically one solid connection. A bad crimp leaves gaps and loose strands, and that's where the resistance builds up, and that's where the heat comes from.

And you couldn't see any of it, because there was a nice neat piece of heat-shrink over the top hiding it.

From what I understand, a bad connection on a cable carrying that much current basically turns into a little heater. Put that together with a cable that was already too small for the job, and that's how you end up with a melted lug inside your bench seat.

### 3. The fuse was in the wrong place

There *was* a fuse, a 300A ANL. But it was mounted about 90cm from the battery. Priya said it should be within about 18cm of the battery.

The way I understand it, the fuse is meant to protect the cable. If something goes wrong anywhere along that cable, you want the fuse right up near the battery, so as much of the cable as possible is on the protected side. With mine sitting 90cm away, almost a metre of that cable was sitting there with no protection at all.

And one more thing I've learned since, which isn't what Priya said, just me reading and trying to understand: the fuse rating is supposed to match the *wire*, not just the inverter. A 300A fuse on a cable that's too small to safely carry 300A isn't going to blow before the cable gets dangerously hot. Ask your electrician about this one, because I'm way out of my depth, but it's worth asking.

### Also: no smoke detector in the back

The only smoke detector in my van was the one in the cab that came with it from the factory. Nothing in the back, where the batteries and the inverter and I and the dogs actually are. I caught it because of the smell and because I happened to see the smoke. If I'd been out of the van grabbing something, or if the dryer had been louder, or if I'd been facing the other way... I try not to think about it too much.

## The part that really got me

Priya pulled up the photos of my damage on her tablet, side by side with thermal camera shots of her own van running the same kind of load. Same type of setup, same kind of power going through it.

Hers barely got warm. Mine had cooked itself.

The difference was wild. Seeing it side by side like that is what made it real for me. It wasn't bad luck. It wasn't the dryer. It was how the thing was put together.

## Tidy is not the same as right

This is the lesson I keep coming back to, and honestly it's the one I'm most embarrassed about.

I trusted the build because it looked tidy. The cables were neatly run. Everything had heat-shrink on it. It was all clean and organized and it looked professional. I remember literally saying "wow, that's so neat" when Darren showed me the battery compartment.

But tidy is not the same as right. A cable can be beautifully routed and still be the wrong size. A lug can have perfect heat-shrink over it and still be a terrible crimp underneath. I wasn't in a position to tell the difference, and I didn't know what questions to ask. That's the whole reason I'm writing this.

## Tasha, and anyone else getting a build done

Tasha, babe, before you pay that deposit, please ask for these things **in writing**. Not "yeah, don't worry about it" in a text, an actual written spec:

- **What size cable** will run from the battery to the inverter? (For a 3000W inverter at 12V, Priya said 2/0 is what she'd expect. If they say 4 AWG, that's what I had.)
- **What fuse** will protect that cable? What rating, what type, and how far from the battery will it be mounted?
- **What tool do they crimp lugs with?** A proper hydraulic or ratcheting lug crimper is what you want to hear. If they're vague about it, that tells you something.
- **Will there be a smoke detector in the back** near the batteries and inverter? (Make them put one there. Or buy one yourself, they're cheap.)
- **Can you see the connections before the heat-shrink goes on?** Or at least photos of them?
- Ask if they'll let an independent electrician inspect the electrical before you sign off on it. A good builder shouldn't have a problem with that.

And this goes for any builder, not just the one who did mine. This is just stuff everyone should be asking. I didn't, and I wish I had.

## A checklist for your own van

These are things you can look at on your own van. **Do all of this with the power fully off.** Battery switch off, inverter off, shore power unplugged, nothing running. If you're not sure how to fully shut everything down, that's your sign to get a pro in instead.

You're not fixing anything here. You're just looking, so you know whether to call someone.

**With everything off:**

1. **Find your main battery-to-inverter cables.** They're usually the thickest cables in your whole setup. Look for the size printed on the jacket. It'll say something like "4 AWG" or "2/0" or "1/0." Write it down.
2. **Check what size your inverter is.** It'll be on a label on the inverter itself. Write that down too, so you can ask an electrician whether the cable matches.
3. **Find your main fuse.** Follow the positive (red) cable from the battery. How far is the fuse from the battery terminal? Grab a tape measure. If it's way more than about 18cm, ask about it.
4. **Look at every lug and connection you can see.** You're looking for discolouration (brown, blue, or black marks on the metal), melted or bubbled plastic, a jacket that's shrunk back from the lug, or anything that just looks scorched.
5. **Gently wiggle the cables at the lug end.** They shouldn't move inside the lug at all. If the wire twists or slides in the lug, that's a bad sign. (Gently. You're not trying to yank anything off.)
6. **Look for heat-shrink that's gone brown, shiny, or bubbly.** Heat-shrink can hide a bad crimp, but sometimes it'll show you that something underneath has been getting hot.
7. **Check that your terminal bolts are snug.** Don't crank on them, just see whether anything's obviously loose. If it is, get a pro to torque it properly.
8. **Sniff.** Seriously. Stick your head in the battery compartment. If you ever smell hot plastic or that sort of sharp electrical smell, take it seriously.
9. **Check your smoke detector situation.** Is there one in the back, near the batteries? Does it actually work? Press the test button.
10. **Check your extinguisher.** Do you have one? Is it in date? Can you reach it from where you groom without climbing past the batteries?

**Then, with a $40 infrared thermometer:**

Everyone should own a cheap infrared thermometer. I got mine for 40 bucks at Canadian Tire, and I wish I'd had one from day one. It's the little point-and-shoot gun kind, where you aim it at something and it tells you the temperature without touching it.

Next time you're running a big load (dryer on high, say), point it at your main cable connections from a safe distance, without touching anything. Do it at the start of the groom and again after you've been running for a while. You're looking for one connection that's way hotter than the others, or anything that keeps climbing. Remember Priya's van: hers *barely got warm.* If yours is getting hot, stop, shut it down, and get someone to look at it.

Again, I'm not an electrician. This list is about knowing when to call one. If anything on it looks off, or you're just not sure, get a pro to look at your van. It's way cheaper than what I'm dealing with now.

## Where I'm at right now

Okay. The honest part.

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main runs with the right size cable, a new fuse block, and a Class T fuse (which Priya says is the proper type for a lithium setup like mine). It's going to take three weeks minimum, because some of the parts are on order.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. Thirty-one. Every one of those is a dog I love and a client who's been nothing but kind about it, but it's also 31 grooms of income that just aren't happening.

Insurance says "maybe." The adjuster is coming Thursday. I'm trying not to get my hopes up either way.

Darren still hasn't gotten back to me.

I'm going to be honest, because this blog has always been honest: I'm scared. My whole income is that van. Rent is due on the 1st. I'm 28, I built this business myself, and right now it's sitting in a shop in Sackville waiting on parts while I refresh my email waiting on an insurance company. Some days I'm fine and some days I'm really not.

But I keep coming back to the fact that it could have been so much worse. Moose could've been in a crate. I could've been out of the van. It could've happened at night in my driveway. It didn't. I smelled it, I saw it, I hit the switch, and everybody walked away. Moose walked away doing zoomies. So I'm trying to hold onto that.

## Thank you

To everyone who's messaged, sent dog photos, offered to lend me equipment, or just checked in: thank you. It's helped more than you know.

To my clients who've been so patient about rescheduling: I'll be back, and your dogs will be getting the fanciest bows I've got.

To Priya: thank you for being straight with me and for taking the time to actually explain it.

To Moose's mom: that coffee. I'm going to remember that coffee forever.

And Tasha, ask for the specs in writing. Please. I love you and I don't want you sitting on anyone's front steps shaking.

I'll post again when the van's back on the road. Hopefully with a big shiny photo of some very fat, very correctly sized cables and a dog who has no idea how much drama happened in that seat.

Check your vans, girls. 🐾

---

*Once more because it matters: I'm a dog groomer, not an electrician. Everything here is my understanding of what a professional explained to me. Please have a qualified electrician (marine or RV electricians are great for this) inspect your setup, especially before you buy or right after a new build.*
